html:
Ñuu Savi, "the land of the rain", is the Mixtec people's own name for their homeland in the mountains of western Oaxaca and nearby Puebla and Guerrero, in southern Mexico. The Aztecs called it Mixtecapan, from which the word Mixtec comes.

In 1492 it was divided into many small kingdoms, each ruled by a lord from a hill town such as Tilantongo, Teposcolula or Tututepec on the coast. Mixtec painters made the screenfold books, or codices, that record the family trees and wars of these lords, above all the 11th century conqueror Eight Deer Jaguar Claw. Their goldwork and turquoise mosaics were among the finest in Mesoamerica. See also Mixtecs and Mixtec Empire.

From the 1450s the Aztec Triple Alliance conquered much of Ñuu Savi and took tribute, though Tututepec stayed free. The Spanish arrived in the 1520s. Mixtec is still spoken by hundreds of thousands of people in Mexico and among migrants in the United States. Their neighbours to the east were the Zapotecs.
